query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting 5 at.% Mo for Ti to form a quinary (Ti0.95Mo0.05)VNbTa refractory-HEA will raise the 1273 K yield strength of TiVNbTa by ≥50 % (≥ 500 MPa) while keeping room-temperature ductility (> 35 % strain) and thermal conductivity (± 10 %) nearly unchanged, because Mo‐induced lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion impede high-temperature dislocation motion without triggering brittle second phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase BCC TiVNbTa alloy produced by arc melting and as-cast solidification, showing dendritic microstructure (≈800 MPa yield strength, ≈40 % compressive strain at 298 K; ≈330 MPa yield and ≈423 MPa compressive strength at 1273 K).
generation.intervention: Replace 5 at.% of Ti with Mo and homogenise at 1200 °C for 24 h to obtain a single-phase BCC (Ti0.95Mo0.05)VNbTa alloy.
generation.conditions: Uniaxial compression tests at 298–1273 K and 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ strain rate; no irradiation; inert atmosphere. Thermal-conductivity measurements at 298–973 K by laser-flash analysis.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniform substitutional Mo atoms generate additional lattice distortion and short-range chemical complexity within the BCC solid solution.
generation.mechanism: Mo’s larger atomic radius and higher melting point raise the Peierls barrier and reduce vacancy-assisted diffusion, slowing dislocation glide and climb at elevated temperature. The enhanced solid-solution strengthening and suppressed recovery retain a higher density of immobile dislocations, thereby increasing high-temperature strength without sacrificing single-phase stability or thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: 0.2 % yield strength ≥ 500 MPa and compressive strength ≥ 650 MPa at 1273 K with ≥ 30 % strain; room-temperature yield ≈ 900 MPa with ≥ 35 % strain; thermal conductivity within ± 10 % of the TiVNbTa baseline across 298–973 K.
generation.baseline: TiVNbTa: 800 MPa yield at 298 K; 330 MPa yield and 423 MPa compressive strength (30 % strain) at 1273 K; ≈40 % room-temperature ductility; reported thermal conductivity ≈ 13–15 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 300 K.
generation.boundary: Mo content ≤ 10 at.% to avoid secondary σ or μ phases; operating temperature 298–1273 K; inert or vacuum environment; compressive strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of strength gain may vary (±20 %) if unforeseen Mo-rich precipitates form or if thermal conductivity is more sensitive to composition than anticipated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloys: (i) baseline TiVNbTa and (ii) modified (Ti0.95Mo0.05)VNbTa. Verify single-phase BCC by XRD and SEM/EDX. Conduct compression tests at 1273 K (1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) and measure 0.2 % yield stress and compressive strength at 30 % strain. Measure room-temperature ductility. Determine thermal conductivity (298–973 K) via laser-flash analysis. Characterise post-test microstructures (TEM) for precipitation or phase separation.
measurements: Compressive strength at 30 % strain and 1273 K
Phase constitution (XRD, TEM) before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if ANY of the following occur: (a) yield strength increase at 1273 K is < 25 % over baseline, (b) thermal conductivity decreases by > 10 % relative to baseline, (c) room-temperature ductility falls below 25 % strain, or (d) secondary brittle phases are detected after homogenisation.
